Reopening: closed automatically by the #352 merge, but the fix is not yet confirmed to resolve this.

#352 **has** shipped and is worth trying — it routes the installer's two scratch files (the CLI zip and the compose pull log) out of `TEMP` and into `IX_HOME`, which comes from `USERPROFILE` in its long form. Since you confirmed that pointing `TEMP`/`TMP` at a path without a space lets the install finish, moving off `TEMP` should fix it. `install.ps1` is served from `main`, so it is live now — no release needed.

But the mechanism the PR described did not hold up, and nobody has reproduced this on a machine with the failing profile, so the issue should stay open until you can confirm. Specifically:

- PowerShell's FileSystem provider **does** resolve 8.3 short segments on both Windows PowerShell 5.1 and 7 — `Test-Path C:\PROGRA~1` returns `True`, and `Get-Item`, `Expand-Archive` and `Remove-Item` all work on a real `WIN10~1` path.
- Your transcript shows the installer reaching `[ok] Extraction complete`. The two provider calls on the zip (`Test-Path -LiteralPath`, `Get-Item -LiteralPath`) run *before* extraction, so they succeeded on that short path.
- `An object at the specified path ... does not exist.` could not be reproduced from any of ~30 path-taking cmdlets, including every one the installer calls on those paths — they report `Cannot find path` instead.

The most likely remaining explanation is that 8.3 alias *creation* is disabled on that volume while `TEMP` still holds a stale short path, so nothing resolves it. #352 fixes that reading too, which is why it shipped.

**If you are able to help confirm**, two things would settle it:

1. Re-run `irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex` on the affected account with `TEMP`/`TMP` back at their original values, and say whether it completes.
2. If it still fails, the full error would pin it:
   ```powershell
   $env:TEMP
   fsutil 8dot3name query C:
   Test-Path $env:TEMP
   $Error[0] | Format-List * -Force
   ```

One small thing worth checking either way: the output above quotes the path as `C:\Users\WIN10\~1`, with a backslash before `~1`. We assumed that is a copy/paste artifact and the real path is `C:\Users\WIN10~1` (the 8.3 alias of `C:\Users\Win 10`), since a literal `~1` directory would be unusual — but if your console really did print it with the backslash, that changes the diagnosis and is worth knowing.

Thanks for the detailed report — the `TEMP`-without-spaces datapoint is what made the fix actionable.

Thank you for the issue — the detail that a space-free TEMP directory worked was the clue that made this diagnosable, and `C:\Users\Win 10` → `C:\Users\WIN10~1` is the whole bug in one line.

The fix is **merged** in #352: the installer was mixing 8.3 short paths with long-path APIs, so it resolved a path it was never asked to write.

**Deliberately keeping this open** rather than auto-closing it. #352 was filed with `Refs #349` instead of `Fixes #349` precisely so merging would not close this before someone confirms it on a real Windows profile with a space in the path — the fix was verified by other means, not on the machine that hit it.

If you get the chance to re-run the installer on that account after the next release, a confirmation here would be very welcome and I will close it out. No obligation — I will get it verified either way.

The fix shipped in #352 and is on `main`: the installer's scratch files (`.cli-staging-<pid>.zip` and its pull log) now live under `$IX_HOME`, which comes from `USERPROFILE` in long form, instead of under `TEMP` — taking the script off the 8.3-shortened path the failure was traced to.

Deliberately merged as `Refs #349` rather than `Fixes`, so this stayed open pending a real run. Worth restating what is *not* established, because it affects how the verification should be read: the mechanism was never reproduced. The provider cmdlets this script calls resolve 8.3 segments fine on both 5.1 and 7, and no cmdlet the installer invokes produces the reported error string. The likeliest remaining explanation is that 8.3 alias creation is disabled on that volume while `TEMP` still carries a stale short path — moving off `TEMP` fixes that reading too, which is why it was worth shipping ahead of the diagnosis.

@RMA1313 — if you still have that machine, a plain `irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex` with `TEMP`/`TMP` left at their defaults would settle it.

One thing this did **not** cover: `ix upgrade` still stages through `os.tmpdir()`, which on Windows is `TEMP` verbatim. If this class of failure is real, it is unfixed there — and would show up as a broken upgrade rather than a broken install.

Verified end to end on a real Windows machine on 2026-08-13. Closing as fixed.

- Windows PowerShell 5.1.26100.9168

- live `irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex`

Docker Compose was stubbed for test isolation so this did not touch the machine's real containers; the live installer download, release ZIP download, PowerShell extraction, directory swap, launcher creation, and CLI execution were all real. The original failure is in that tested CLI path.

This confirms #352 fixes the installer even when `TEMP` is unusable, not merely when it contains a space. #392 also moved `ix upgrade` downloads off `TEMP`, covering the related upgrade path.

Thank you for the issue — and for fixing it in the same breath. The report is precise about the mechanism (definitions landing in a later streamed batch than the caller), which is what made #375 straightforward to review against.

Tracked by **#375**, which is open with review comments. It carries `Fixes #374`, so this will close automatically when that lands.

The change itself is correct — the index construction mirrors `resolveEdges`' in-batch path exactly, so cross-batch and in-batch resolution agree on `dstQualifiedKey`. My open question is cost, not correctness: the prescan parses synchronously on the main thread while the streaming loop uses a worker pool, so every unchanged JS/TS file is re-read and re-parsed on each incremental `ix map`. Details and measurements are on the PR.

Thank you for the issue — this is a real gap, and one that quietly corrupts the graph rather than failing loudly, which makes it worth more than its size suggests.

Tracked by **#378**, which is open with review comments and currently conflicting with `main`. It carries `Fixes #377`, so this will close automatically when that lands.

The approach is right (compare the previous patch manifest, emit explicit deletions, track dependents so a recreated file heals its callers). The blocking item on the PR is that `reconcileRemovedEntities` runs before `stripMapModeOps`, which means `ix map` after `ix ingest` deletes chunk nodes it never recreates — reproduced on the branch. Detail on the PR.

Thank you for the issue. You framed the underlying principle exactly right: `--kind` is a *filter*, not a *tiebreaker*, and silently analysing the wrong symbol is worse than asking which one was meant.

Tracked by **#380**, which is approved and carries `Fixes #379`, so this will close automatically when it lands.

Both causes are now covered, in the plugin repo — mirrored there as ix-codex-plugin#22, because GitHub closing keywords do not work across repositories and this issue would otherwise never auto-close.

| cause | fix |
|---|---|
| `/bin/sh -lc` in all five `hooks.json` commands | ix-codex-plugin#20 |

Leaving this open. Neither PR has been run on real Windows; both were written and tested on Linux, where the changed paths are no-ops or unit-tested in isolation. @tept-creator — a confirmation from a real Windows box after both merge is what should close this.

Thank you for the issue — this is an unusually good report. Naming the exact path the wrapper tried to execute is what made it diagnosable in one pass, and noting that reinstalling restored it confirmed the cause before anyone had to reproduce it.

## Unblocking you now

```powershell
irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex
```

That rewrites the launcher and restores the CLI, which matches what you already found. You should not need to uninstall first, and your graph and config are untouched — the breakage is only in `~\.ix\bin\ix.cmd`.

## What happened

You were on the wrong side of a one-way door.

`ix upgrade` before 0.9.0 refreshed only the **bash** shim (the one Git Bash uses) and never touched `~\.ix\bin\ix.cmd`, which is the launcher native PowerShell actually runs. Meanwhile the upgrade extracted the new CLI into a **version-nested** directory, so `~\.ix\cli\ix.cmd` — the path your launcher points at — stopped existing. Your wrapper was left aimed at a file the upgrade had just moved.

The layout half of this was fixed in #346 and shipped in v0.9.0. The catch is that `ix upgrade` is run by the version you are upgrading *from*, so 0.8.1 executed 0.8.1's code and the fix could not participate. **Anyone going from ≤0.8.1 to 0.9.x on Windows hits this**, and no change we ship can prevent it retroactively — which is precisely why it deserved its own fix rather than a "already fixed, please upgrade" reply.

Once you are on 0.9.1, future upgrades go through `refreshLaunchers()`, which rewrites the launcher for either layout. This is a one-time cost.

## What is changing

#386 makes the launcher diagnose itself. It checks its target before invoking it and, when it is missing, prints the cause and the reinstall command instead of cmd.exe's message naming the wrapper. That has to live in the batch file: at that point `ix doctor` is exactly as unreachable as `ix`, so nothing inside the CLI can reach you.

Your report also turned up a second bug in the same three lines: the old launcher never propagated the exit code, so **every** non-zero `ix` exit was reported to callers as success. That has been fixed alongside it.

I am leaving this issue open until someone confirms the new launcher on real Windows — I do not have a machine to run cmd.exe on, and I would rather not close it on tests alone.

One question, if you have a moment: does `ix --version` report `0.9.1` after reinstalling? That tells us whether the upgrade had already staged the new CLI correctly and only the launcher was wrong, or whether the payload needed replacing too.

Status check, since three separate changes touch this and it is not obvious from the outside which of them closes it.

**The forward path is complete.** Traced end to end on `main`:

- the release archive carries `ix.cmd` at its top level (`release.yml:309`), so the file the shim targets is genuinely in the tarball;
- `install.ps1` collapses that top level into a flat `$IX_HOME\cli\`, which is why `%~dp0..\cli\ix.cmd` resolves (#346, v0.9.0);
- `ix upgrade` re-derives the same layout — `soleChildDir(installDir) ?? installDir` (`upgrade.ts:1026`) — and `refreshLaunchers()` rewrites `bin\ix.cmd` to match, flat or nested, on every upgrade.

So an upgrade **from v0.9.0 or later** rewrites the shim to a target that exists.

**What cannot be fixed forward** is the population this was reported from: `ix upgrade` is executed by the version being upgraded *from*, so nothing shipped today reaches a v0.8.1 install. #386 is the recovery for exactly that — the launcher now checks its target before invoking it and prints the reinstall command, because once broken, `ix doctor` is as unreachable as `ix`.

**What is still missing is a Windows run.** Every piece above is asserted by tests and has never been executed by `cmd.exe` — #386 shipped as `Refs`, not `Fixes`, for that reason. This wants:

1. a v0.9.1 → v0.9.2 upgrade, confirming `ix --version` still works afterwards, and
2. a deliberately broken `bin\ix.cmd` (point it at a nonexistent target), confirming the recovery message prints rather than the raw `is not recognized` error.

That is what should close this, not another patch. Same standing requirement as #349 and #383.

Verified on native Windows on 2026-08-13. Closing as fixed.

Environment:
- Windows 11 Home, build 26200
- Windows PowerShell 5.1 for installation; PowerShell 7.6.4 for upgrade/launcher checks
- Node v26.7.0

Forward-upgrade check:

1. Used the live installer with `IX_VERSION=0.9.1` to create a fresh, working install under the spaced profile path `C:\Users\josep\Ix 385 Test`.
2. Restricted PATH to that isolated `bin\ix.cmd`, Node, Windows tools, and a Docker stub. `where ix` returned only the isolated launcher; the real npm launcher was SHA-256 checked before and after and stayed byte-identical.

   - `ix --version` afterwards returned `0.9.3` with exit 0

This is the requested v0.9.1→newer forward-path check, using v0.9.3 rather than v0.9.2 because that is now the current release.

Broken-launcher recovery check:

1. Re-ran the live v0.9.3 installer so `bin\ix.cmd` contained #386's current self-diagnosing body.
2. Temporarily moved `$IX_HOME\cli\ix.cmd` aside and invoked `bin\ix.cmd` through PowerShell/cmd.exe.

The original ≤0.8.1 one-way upgrade cannot be changed retroactively, as discussed above, but both the supported forward path and #386 recovery behavior are now confirmed on Windows.

Pushed the fixes to this branch rather than sending you round another loop — everything below is on `0c9087c`, and the original commit is untouched underneath it so nothing you wrote is lost.

**Scoped it to the two pieces that belong in this repo:** the `ix` skill and the API reference. The API docs I would have taken as-is; they hold up (39 paths, 13 schemas, every path grounded in the backend routes).

**Moved out**, because the layer was wrong rather than the code:

- `skills/ix/scripts/compass-patch/` — the reasons are in the commit message, but the short version is that this repo owns `view.ts`, so patching its *compiled* output is fighting the build, and `fit-view.js` was writing the exact two inline styles React drives from `snappedZoom`/`snappedPan`.
- `upstream/compass-fit-view/` — nothing here builds React.

**Both are worth landing in `system-compass`, and I would review that PR.** The F-key fit view is genuinely new there — Compass binds `0` for reset-zoom and nothing binds `F`. Your `upstream/` port is most of the work already. What I would drop is the auto-frame-on-load: Compass #57 fixed the empty-first-paint upstream and it ships in v0.9.1, so that part is solved. The F key is not.

**Two bugs found while testing your scripts, both fixed here:**

- `version_ge` in `bootstrap.sh` was inverted. `sort -C` succeeds when input is *already ordered*, so want-then-got asks "is want <= got" — the `-r` asked the reverse. Node 22.22.2 against a floor of 22 printed "Ix requires Node >= 22", and Node 18 passed silently. I hit it dry-running your bootstrap on this machine. Checked across 22.22.2 / 24 / 22.0.0 / 20.11.1 / 18.4.0.
- `install-skill.sh` `rm -rf`d the destination unconditionally. `ix` is a short name, and a hand-written skill that happened to share it went without a prompt or a backup. It now refuses unless the destination carries `name: ix`, with `--force` to override. Tested all four paths: clean install, re-install, squatted name, and `--force`.

Also: `C:/Users/jacob/...` out of CLAUDE.md, the two gitignored paths out of its layout table, `/dist/` anchored, and the `POST /__ix/remap` section in the API docs now says what actually happens (falls through to the SPA handler, returns index.html with a 200) rather than describing the patched behaviour.

**Kept, with credit:** the global-`ix reset` warning and `registerPatchesCommand` never being registered. The second is now #371 — a good catch, it had been sitting there unnoticed because `patches` is in `PRO_COMMANDS`, so OSS users get "requires Ix Pro" instead of an unknown-command error.

Re-reviewing now. Thanks for a genuinely careful first contribution — the fact that everything in your description checked out when I ran it is not the norm.

Rebased onto `main` and pushed the fix for the blocking item, so this is unblocked from my side.

**Note the conflict**: #382 landed while this was open and touched the same three places — `INDEX_PRESCAN_EXTENSIONS`, the parser-derived block in `buildGlobalResolutionIndex`, and `resolveEdges.test.ts`. I merged both rather than picking a side: the prescan set is now `.go .php .r .sas` + the six JS/TS extensions, and both cross-batch tests are kept.

## The perf fix

Your design decision — derive the index from real parse results rather than a regex, so it cannot drift from what the in-batch path extracts — is right, and I did not want to trade it away. The problem was only *where* the parsing happened: a synchronous main-thread loop inside `buildGlobalResolutionIndex`.

`buildGlobalResolutionIndex` now takes an optional `preParsed` map, and the CLI parses prescan sources on **the worker pool it is already running** for the streaming loop, handing the results in. Absent an entry, each language block falls back to parsing in-index, so tests and library callers behave exactly as before.

Measured on this repo, 180 JS/TS files:

```
index WITHOUT preParsed (main-thread parse): 1.24 s
index WITH preParsed (pool did the work):    0.001 s
```

The parse work still happens — it moved to the pool and spreads across cores instead of blocking. Applied to PHP, R and SAS too, since all four blocks had the same shape.

Added a test that supplies a parse result whose entity does not appear in the source text: it can only resolve if `preParsed` is genuinely used rather than re-parsed.

## Verification

- `core-ingestion`: **35 passed** in `resolveEdges.test.ts`; full suite 280 passed with the same 6 pre-existing failures you documented, no new ones
- `ix-cli`: **698 passed** across 52 files, `npm run typecheck` clean, lint 0 errors / 38 pre-existing warnings

## Still open, and worth its own issue rather than this PR

An incremental map still parses every prescanned file, not just the changed ones — it is parallel now instead of serial, but a one-file edit in a 5,000-file TypeScript repo still does 5,000 parses. The real fix is caching the per-file index keyed on mtime so unchanged files are never re-parsed, which needs cache invalidation and is a bigger change than belongs here. I'd rather land this and file that separately than hold a correct fix behind an optimisation.

I amended your commit rather than stacking, since the fix is threaded through the same lines; you are still the author and I added myself as co-author. Shout if you would rather it were split.

Rebased onto `main` (clean this time — #382/#384/#386/#387 landed since) and pushed fixes for the blocking item and two of the "please reconsider" points, as `d827cc9`. Your commits are intact; mine sits on top.

## 1. The blocker — map mode was destroying chunk data

`stripMapModeOps` drops every chunk `UpsertNode` but leaves `DeleteNode` alone, and `chunkId` hashes the chunk's start line. So any edit that shifts lines made every downstream chunk look removed, and `ix map` after an `ix ingest` deleted the file's chunks without recreating them — the cheap command silently destroying what the expensive one built.

`reconcileRemovedEntities` now takes a `mapMode` flag and leaves chunk nodes and `CONTAINS_CHUNK`/`NEXT` edges alone. The kind comes from the `client.entity()` lookup **you were already making** for incident edges, so it costs no extra round trip — that turned out to be the neat part of your design, not something I had to work around.

Three tests: chunks untouched in map mode, still deleted outside it, and chunk-carrying edges spared while a `CALLS` edge on the same node is still removed.

## 2. Empty-baseline guard — restored, but scoped

You dropped `mtimes.size === 0` so that deleting the last mapped file could persist an empty baseline. That case is real, but the guard was load-bearing for a different one: there is no `filePaths.length === 0` check anywhere in `ingestFiles`, so *any* discovery failure — over-broad ignore rule, wrong cwd — now overwrote a good baseline with an empty one.

It now asks **why** the map is empty: with deletions recorded this run, empty is a real state and is persisted; without them, discovery is assumed to have gone wrong and the baseline is kept. Your "persists an empty baseline after the last mapped file is deleted" test still passes unchanged, and I added its mirror image.

## 3. Fail-closed lookup — kept, narrowed

Failing closed before deleting is right; deleting from an unreliable baseline is how data gets lost. But letting the throw escape aborted the entire map over one transient blip, taking the ordinary ingest of every changed file with it. The deletions are now dropped for that run — they stay in the baseline and retry next time — and the rest proceeds.

## Verification

- `ix-cli`: **710 passed** across 53 files (was 693), typecheck clean, lint 0 errors / 38 pre-existing warnings
- `core-ingestion`: 279 passed with the same 6 pre-existing failures, no new ones

## Left alone deliberately

- **Per-file round trips.** `sourcePatchIdCandidates` returns 25 ids tried serially, plus one `client.entity()` per removed node. Real, but batching it is a separate change and I did not want to bury the correctness fixes underneath it.
- **Op ordering.** `DeleteNode` still precedes the trailing `DeleteEdge`s for incident edges. I could not answer from the CLI side whether the backend cascades incident-edge removal on node delete — if it does, those trailing deletes target rows that are already gone. Worth confirming before anyone calls the ordering intentional.
- **Baseline write amplification.** `onCommitted` rewrites the whole baseline per deleted file. Bounded, and per-file durability is a defensible trade.

I'm happy with this now aside from those. If you'd rather take the round-trip batching yourself, say so and I'll leave it; otherwise I can follow up separately.

**What changed** — only `core-ingestion/src/queries.ts` and `queries.php.test.ts`. Your commit is untouched.
